turns.doctor_question: Hello, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi. Nice to meet you too. Um, I'm here because... well, I just can't stop seeing this droop and unevenness around my mouth and my jaw. 

Every time I catch a reflection or see a photo of myself, it's all I can focus on. People keep telling me I look fine, but... it just feels so incredibly obvious to me. It's gotten so bad that I've actually started avoiding client meetings and presentations at work, so I knew I needed to come in and talk to someone.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient is preoccupied with a perceived droop and asymmetry around their mouth and jaw that others state is not noticeable, causing functional impairment.

turns.doctor_question: How certain are you that the droop and unevenness are truly noticeable to other people?
turns.patient_response:
Well, like I was saying, people do tell me I look fine. So I hear them when they say that. But... to me, I'm just absolutely certain it's there. It's glaring. 

Whenever I see a photo or catch my reflection, that droop is literally the only thing I can see. It feels so incredibly obvious that I just assume everyone else must be noticing it too, even if they're just being polite. That's exactly why I've been backing out of my client meetings and presentations at work. I just can't stand up in front of people feeling like they're staring at my uneven jaw.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient expresses an intense preoccupation with a perceived droop and asymmetry around their mouth and jaw that others tell them is not noticeable, to the point where it impairs their work functioning.

turns.doctor_question: Can you consider that your perception of the droop might be exaggerated or not actually noticeable, or are you completely convinced it is truly there?
turns.patient_response: I know what you're asking, but... no, I'm completely convinced it's there. I mean, I hear what people say, but I just can't stop seeing it. Every single time I look in a mirror or see a picture, the droop around my mouth and the unevenness in my jaw is right there. It's so obvious to me. It's why I can't face clients or do presentations anymore. I just can't shake the feeling that it's glaringly obvious, no matter what anyone else says.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes a persistent, unshakeable preoccupation with perceived flaws in facial appearance (droop around the mouth and jaw unevenness) that others dismiss, which leads to avoidance of clients and presentations.

turns.doctor_question: How often do you check mirrors or photos specifically to inspect the droop or unevenness around your mouth and jaw?
turns.patient_response:
It's a lot. Honestly, before I leave for work or if we have any kind of family event, I can spend hours just checking the bathroom mirror. I'll take pictures on my phone from different angles to see how it looks, and then I end up redoing my makeup or adjusting my scarf trying to hide it. 

I also ask my husband constantly if my face looks lopsided... and I'll even sit there scrolling through photos of other women just to see how bad my jaw looks beside theirs. So, it takes up a huge amount of my time.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient describes spending hours checking mirrors, taking photos from multiple angles, camouflaging with makeup and scarves, seeking constant reassurance from her husband, and comparing her appearance to other women.

turns.doctor_question: When you avoid meetings and presentations, is it mainly because of your concern about the perceived droop and unevenness, or because you generally fear being judged or embarrassed in social situations?
turns.patient_response:
It's definitely because of my face. I mean, I've been an architect for years, so I'm completely used to presenting designs and running client meetings. I never used to have a problem with it, and I don't have a general fear of talking to people or being judged on my work. 

It's really just... I can't stand the thought of them sitting there staring at my mouth and my uneven jaw while I speak. If my face didn't look like this, I'd be in those meetings right now without a second thought. So, yeah, it's strictly because of the droop.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient confirms that their avoidance and distress are strictly driven by preoccupation with perceived flaws in their facial appearance, specifically their mouth, uneven jaw, and droop.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from your concern about your mouth and jaw, do you have any other beliefs that people around you say are clearly untrue?
turns.patient_response: No, not at all. It's just... it's just my face. I don't have any other strange beliefs or anything like that. People don't tell me I'm making things up about other stuff. It's really only when I talk about how my mouth and jaw look that my husband or my friends tell me I'm wrong. But other than that, no.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly denies having delusions or other strange beliefs that people tell them are untrue.
